BEGINNER1. What is Playwright?

Playwright is a modern, open-source end-to-end testing framework created by Microsoft. A single API drives three browser engines — Chromium (Chrome/Edge), Firefox, and WebKit (Safari) — so one test file can validate your app across the entire browser landscape without rewriting anything per browser.

Unlike older tools that bolted a test runner and assertion library onto a browser driver, Playwright ships all three as one cohesive package: @playwright/test. You get a test runner, an expect() assertion library with auto-retrying matchers, parallel execution, and rich debugging artifacts (screenshots, video, traces) out of the box.

Why teams choose Playwright: auto-waiting eliminates most manual sleep() calls, a single install script downloads matching browser binaries (no version-mismatch surprises), and the Trace Viewer lets you time-travel through a failed test step by step.

Playwright vs. Alternatives

Feature Playwright Selenium Cypress
Browser engines Chromium, Firefox, WebKit Any via WebDriver Chromium-family, Firefox
Auto-waiting ✅ Built in ❌ Manual waits ✅ Built in
Multi-tab / multi-origin ✅ Native ⚠️ Clunky ❌ Limited
Built-in test runner ✅ Yes ❌ No (needs JUnit/TestNG) ✅ Yes
True parallelism ✅ Multi-process workers ⚠️ Grid setup required ⚠️ Paid dashboard for parallel

BEGINNER2. Bootstrapping with npm init playwright@latest

The fastest way to start a new project is the official scaffolding wizard. It installs dependencies, downloads browsers, and generates a working example — all in one command.

npm init playwright@latest

The wizard asks four questions:

  • TypeScript or JavaScript? — TypeScript is the default and recommended choice
  • Name of your Tests folder — defaults to tests (or e2e)
  • Add a GitHub Actions workflow? — scaffolds .github/workflows/playwright.yml
  • Install Playwright browsers now? — downloads Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit
💡 Tip: You can add Playwright to an existing project the same way — the wizard detects your package manager (npm, yarn, or pnpm) and merges into your existing package.json rather than overwriting it.

Adding to an Existing Project Manually

npm install -D @playwright/test
npx playwright install

BEGINNER3. The Generated Project Structure

After the wizard finishes, you'll see a predictable layout:

my-project/
├── tests/
│   └── example.spec.ts        # sample test — safe to delete
├── tests-examples/
│   └── demo-todo-app.spec.ts  # richer reference example
├── playwright.config.ts       # central configuration
├── package.json
└── .github/
    └── workflows/
        └── playwright.yml      # CI workflow (if you opted in)

Minimal playwright.config.ts

import { defineConfig, devices } from '@playwright/test';

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests',
  timeout: 30_000,
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,
  reporter: 'html',
  use: {
    baseURL: 'http://localhost:3000',
    trace: 'on-first-retry',
  },
  projects: [
    { name: 'chromium', use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] } },
    { name: 'firefox',  use: { ...devices['Desktop Firefox'] } },
    { name: 'webkit',   use: { ...devices['Desktop Safari'] } },
  ],
});
What each piece does: testDir tells Playwright where to look for spec files, use.baseURL lets every test call page.goto('/login') instead of a full URL, and projects defines which browser engines every test runs against.

BEGINNER4. Installing and Managing Browsers

Playwright doesn't use the browsers already installed on your machine — it downloads its own tested, pinned versions of Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit so tests behave identically on every developer machine and CI runner.

npx playwright install                # all three browsers
npx playwright install chromium       # just one
npx playwright install --with-deps    # + OS-level libraries (needed on fresh Linux CI images)
⚠️ Common Pitfall: On a fresh Ubuntu CI image, npx playwright install alone often fails at runtime with missing shared library errors. Always use --with-deps in Linux CI containers — it installs the OS packages (fonts, codecs, GTK libraries) that the browsers need to actually launch.

Where Browsers Are Stored

Downloaded browsers live in a shared cache directory (~/.cache/ms-playwright on Linux/macOS, %USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\ms-playwright on Windows) — not inside node_modules. This means multiple projects on the same machine reuse the same binaries instead of re-downloading them.

BEGINNER5. Running Tests from the CLI

npx playwright test                    # run every test
npx playwright test login.spec.ts      # a single file
npx playwright test --headed           # show the browser window
npx playwright test --grep "checkout"  # filter by title text
npx playwright test --project=chromium # run one browser project only
npx playwright test --workers=4        # cap parallel workers
Headless (default, CI-friendly): 
npx playwright test
# No visible window; fastest execution
Headed (local debugging): 
npx playwright test --headed
# Opens a real browser window you can watch

INTERMEDIATE6. UI Mode and Debug Mode

Two interactive modes make failures far easier to diagnose than reading terminal output alone.

UI Mode

npx playwright test --ui

Opens a visual dashboard: a list of every test, a timeline you can scrub through, and a "watch mode" that re-runs tests automatically as you edit files. Each step shows a DOM snapshot — you can literally see what the page looked like when a locator resolved (or failed to).

Debug Mode

npx playwright test --debug
npx playwright test login.spec.ts --debug   # scoped to one file

Launches the Playwright Inspector, which pauses before the first action and lets you step through the test line by line, inspect locators live against the running page, and even generate new locators by clicking on the page.

💡 Tip: Add await page.pause() anywhere in a test to drop into the Inspector at that exact point, without running the whole file in --debug mode.

INTERMEDIATE7. The HTML Reporter

npx playwright test --reporter=html
npx playwright show-report            # serves the last report locally

The HTML report is a self-contained, shareable artifact — attach screenshots, embedded videos, and full traces for every failed test, all viewable in a browser with zero server setup beyond show-report's built-in static server.

Reporter Best for
html Local review and CI artifact upload — rich, interactive
dot Fast local runs — one character per test
list Verbose console output showing every test title
junit Feeding results into non-native CI dashboards
github Inline PR annotations on GitHub Actions

ADVANCED8. Setting Up Continuous Integration

A CI workflow needs to install dependencies, download browsers with their OS libraries, run the suite, and preserve the report as a downloadable artifact — especially important because a failed CI run's HTML report is often the only way to diagnose an environment-specific failure.

name: Playwright Tests
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20 }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps
      - run: npx playwright test
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: always()
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: playwright-report/
          retention-days: 30
Why if: always() matters: without it, the artifact upload step is skipped whenever tests fail — which is exactly the moment you most need the report. if: always() makes the upload run regardless of the test step's outcome.

package.json Convenience Scripts

{
  "scripts": {
    "test":        "npx playwright test",
    "test:headed": "npx playwright test --headed",
    "test:ui":     "npx playwright test --ui",
    "test:debug":  "npx playwright test --debug",
    "report":      "npx playwright show-report"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@playwright/test": "^1.48.0"
  }
}

ADVANCED9. Common Setup Pitfalls

⚠️ Pitfall 1 — Version drift: @playwright/test and the downloaded browser binaries must stay in lockstep. If you bump the npm package version, always re-run npx playwright install so the binaries match. Mismatched versions can cause confusing, hard-to-reproduce failures.
⚠️ Pitfall 2 — Forgetting --with-deps on Linux: Docker images and minimal CI runners frequently lack the shared libraries WebKit and Firefox need. The error message ("error while loading shared libraries") is a strong signal to add --with-deps.
⚠️ Pitfall 3 — No baseURL configured: Without use.baseURL in the config, every page.goto('/path') call throws because Playwright has no origin to resolve the relative path against. Set it once in the config instead of hardcoding full URLs in every test.

Checking Your Installed Version

npx playwright --version

📋 Quick Reference Summary

Concept Key Points
Scaffold npm init playwright@latest — generates config, sample test, optional CI workflow.
Browsers npx playwright install [--with-deps] — Playwright manages its own pinned binaries.
Run tests npx playwright test, with --headed, --grep, --project, --workers flags.
Debugging --ui for a visual dashboard, --debug or page.pause() for step-by-step Inspector.
Reporting --reporter=html + npx playwright show-report for a shareable, interactive report.
CI Install with --with-deps, always upload the report artifact with if: always().
